newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lower wheat prices seen easing EU refund pressure.
newsitem.headline: Lower wheat prices seen easing EU refund pressure.

text.p: Lower domestic grain prices point to a lower European Union export refund for wheat this week, grain traders and analysts said on Tuesday.
The fall in prices, helped along by currency movements, is likely to please the European Commission, which is pushing for a low-refund campaign coupled with competitive domestic prices, they said.
"The dollar is higher this week and internal prices are down so you're looking at a lower restitution," a French trader said.
The Commission on Friday told farmers that internal prices were too high given the big 200-million-tonne total grain crop, and officials were driving the message home again on Tuesday.
A Commission official earlier told Reuters in Brussels "The high internal price is inexplicable. There is going to be a good harvest but farmers don't appear to have got the message."
But despite some speculation that the EU might be looking at fresh export restrictions to knock domestic prices, officials said there was no talk of another retreat from world markets.

"We never said that," an EU source said on Tuesday, adding that a trade circular summarising a consultative meeting between the Commission and the industry on Friday gave a clear picture of current EU policy.

Brussels-based grain trade association Coceral said in its summary of the meeting "The Commission wishes to export as much as possible but the restitutions must be as low as possible. That is only achievable if internal prices fall."
The EU restricted wheat and barley exports through export taxes last year but has returned to a policy of export refunds to bridge a gap between local prices and lower prices elsewhere.

Well-placed sources said the Commission was understood to be concerned that EU prices, although lower than last year, had not fallen even further given the increase of more than 10 percent in both wheat and total grain harvests this year.
They said prices had been especially slow to react in France, where prices for barley and standard wheat are almost identical. Wheat is some seven percent above EU intervention.
The EU was therefore likely to be especially attentive to the level of refunds demanded by the trade, they said.
"Each Ecu off the internal price is one less Ecu the Commission has to give in restitution," one source noted.
Sensitivities about refund levels have not been eased by a run-in with the United States over the EU's decision to restore wheat export subsidies in September, analysts said.
The U.S. has hinted that current EU wheat refunds of six Ecus per tonne are not alarming enough to spark a subsidy war.
But it says it will roll out its own grain export subsidies again if necessary to meet aggressive EU competition.
In a bid to soothe its traditional rival, Brussels has vowed not to undercut U.S. wheat with high export refunds.

The EU last week exported just under 200,000 tonnes of soft wheat at a refund of 6.49 Ecus. Since then French wheat has lost about one percent, the dollar has gained 0.6 percent and U.S. wheat prices have risen slightly -- all saving subsidy costs.
Traders said a notional EU refund of some five Ecus per tonne was now needed to match prices for U.S. soft red winter. Traders bid for the refunds at weekly tenders each Thursday.
